paras: The threatened lynching of Ed and Rosa Hutcheson took place at Stevenson, Jackson County, Alabama, on July 19, 1903, when about fifty men closed around the Black couple as an officer hurried them onto a train after their arrest. The couple, charged with writing an obscene letter to the daughter of a prominent Stevenson man, were jailed under armed guard at Scottsboro and later fined $500 and sentenced to six months' hard labor. Rosa Hutcheson escaped with her infant after sentencing and was recaptured soon afterward.

Ed Hutcheson and his wife, Rosa, were arrested at Stevenson late on Sunday afternoon, July 19, on a charge of writing an obscene letter to Miss Foster, the young daughter of Thomas Foster, a former tax assessor described as "one of the most prominent men in the county." The Scottsboro correspondent wrote that "it was known" the couple had written the letter and signed it with the name of John Rice, another Black man, "to get revenge."

According to the correspondent, the letter so angered "a number of the citizens of Stevenson" that a mob was feared. Sheriff Austin and Solicitor Proctor were told by telephone, and the sheriff ordered the officer holding the prisoners to get them away at once. About fifty men were closing around the couple as they were "hustled aboard" the midnight train to Scottsboro.

At Scottsboro the sheriff put them in jail and posted heavily armed guards, and the next morning he and the solicitor went to Stevenson to investigate. A dispatch of July 21 reported the couple "safely in jail," said the people, "while greatly incensed," were "disposed to await the action of the courts," and noted that guards remained as a precaution.

The couple were tried at Scottsboro before C. L. Cargill, judge of probate, and were fined $500 and sentenced to six months' hard labor for the county, which the Montgomery Advertiser called "the full limit of the law." No arrest of anyone in the crowd at Stevenson is reported in the coverage.

While the prisoners waited at night for a late train, Rosa, with her infant in her arms, slipped away from the guard, and Sheriff Austin offered a $10 reward for her capture. A later Age-Herald item said Perry Pipps brought bloodhounds from Chattanooga, but Constable Darwin captured her first, after she had covered about 25 miles in one night with the baby. That item also described her as convicted "on two charges."

The episode appeared only in white Alabama dailies, through near-identical Scottsboro specials in the Birmingham Age-Herald and the Montgomery Advertiser from July 21 to July 31. Headlines put the mob first, with "NEGROES BARELY ESCAPE ANGRY MOB" in the Age-Herald and "NEGROES IN DANGER / JACKSON MOB AFTER MAN AND WIFE" in the Advertiser, and the Age-Herald expressed hope that "good counsel will prevail and a lynching be averted." Both papers nonetheless stated the couple's guilt as known before any hearing, and the Age-Herald described the "indignation" over the "insulting letter" without criticism.
The trial and the escape were reported as brief items in Scottsboro news columns, among weddings, funerals and land suits.

The reports differ on the trial date: the Advertiser placed it on Monday, July 27, the day set for the preliminary hearing, while the Age-Herald's July 29 dispatch said "yesterday." The earlier reports said Rosa slipped away from the guard while awaiting the train, whereas the July 31 Age-Herald said she "escaped from jail last Tuesday night." The surname was also printed as Hutcheson, Hutcherson and Hutchinson.

accounts.label: Scottsboro correspondent
accounts.gist: The couple wrote an obscene letter to a prominent man's daughter; Stevenson citizens were infuriated, fifty men closed in at the train, and quick action by the sheriff averted a lynching.

accounts.label: Scottsboro correspondent, follow-ups
accounts.gist: The couple were convicted and given the maximum sentence; Rosa escaped with her baby and was run down with bloodhounds.

framing.detail: Headlines such as 'NEGROES BARELY ESCAPE ANGRY MOB' and 'JACKSON MOB AFTER MAN AND WIFE' reported the threat and the hope that 'good counsel will prevail', while treating the couple's guilt as 'known' and the indignation as natural.
Follow-ups were short items in Scottsboro news columns, set among weddings, deaths and land suits.
